title: The Housemaid
synopsis: You took the live-in housekeeping job because nobody else would hire someone with your record. The Winchesters' attic locks from the outside. You'll find out why.

nodes.text: The photos undersold it. Gravel somebody rakes, a lawn with stripes in it, and a door that opens before you knock. Nina Winchester smiles the way people smile in the second take. Andrew carries your duffel in himself, and the bag looks wrong in that foyer — a nylon thing under a chandelier. Nobody asks about the four-year gap in your resume. That's the part that worries you.

choices.text: Be cheerful and grateful
choices.consequence: You give them the version of yourself that got the interview: bright, harmless, easy to forget. Nina relaxes. Andrew doesn't, quite.

choices.text: Be polite and observant
choices.consequence: You keep your answers short and count exits instead. Four years in a place with locked doors teaches you to read a house before you unpack in it.

nodes.text: Nina walks you through twelve rooms she seems to be seeing for the first time — she calls the study 'the, um, the office one' and laughs at herself. Andrew stays a step behind, always a step, like a man checking your work. At the end of the upstairs hall a narrow door opens onto stairs. She doesn't touch the switch beside it. She keeps talking, faster, all the way back down.

choices.text: Ask about the attic directly
choices.consequence: You ask what's up there and watch two faces do two different things. Nina says 'storage.' Andrew says 'your room.' They say it at the same time.

choices.text: Note it silently and move on
choices.consequence: You let the door go unmentioned and file away the switch she wouldn't touch. Some questions are worth more unasked, and you have been here twenty minutes.

nodes.text: She hands you a typed list — actual typewriter, the letters bitten into the paper. Twenty-three rules. Number nine specifies which cloth for the marble. Number fourteen forbids using Andrew's mug. Number six reads: Do not enter the attic for any reason. Number seven reads: You will sleep in the attic. Nina watches you read them in order and waits to see which one you'll mention.

choices.text: Sign and ask no questions
choices.consequence: You sign under twenty-three rules that contradict each other twice and hand the pen back smiling. She takes it like you passed something.

choices.text: Ask gentle, clarifying questions
choices.consequence: You ask which rule wins when two disagree. Nina says 'whichever one Andrew remembers,' then checks the doorway to make sure it's empty.

nodes.text: The attic holds heat like a closed car. One window, painted shut in a previous decade. A mattress, a lamp, a hook where a mirror used to hang. The door has a deadbolt on the outside and the brass is bright — installed recently, by someone who measured twice. Below you, a marriage argues in the register people use when they think the house absorbs it. It doesn't. Not up here.

choices.text: Try the door to see if it really locks
choices.consequence: You try the handle at one in the morning and it opens, which should be a relief. You lie awake anyway, listening for the sound of somebody deciding.

choices.text: Sit very still and listen
choices.consequence: You don't touch the door. You sit on the mattress in the dark and learn the argument by heart — three voices, and one of them is nine years old.

nodes.text: Cecelia is nine and the only person in this house who looks directly at you. She has her mother's face and her father's stillness, and she eats her cereal in exactly nine spoonfuls, counting under her breath. At breakfast she slides a square of folded paper across the marble with two fingers, keeps eating, and never glances up. She has done this before. That's the part that stops you.

choices.text: Read the note when alone
choices.consequence: In the pantry you unfold four words in careful pencil: DON'T BE ALONE WITH HIM. No name. A nine-year-old chose not to write the name.

choices.text: Burn the note and never speak of it
choices.consequence: You burn it over the sink without reading past the first line, because knowing makes you a witness. The ash goes down the drain. It stays with you anyway.

nodes.text: Andrew develops reasons to be in the kitchen at ten in the morning. He praises your coffee, then your hands, then — casually, reaching past you for a glass — the eighteen months you spent in a facility outside Bedford Hills. He read the file. He wants you to know he read the file. He says 'I don't judge' the way other men say 'I own this.'

choices.text: Hold a hard line on professional distance
choices.consequence: You answer in job titles and step-lengths, never less than a meter, never after seven. He finds it funny for four days. On the fifth he stops finding it funny.

choices.text: Pretend to laugh along while building a plan
choices.consequence: You laugh at the right beats and hate the sound of it. Being underestimated is a tool. You have used it before and it worked.

nodes.text: A jar of apricot preserve goes off the pantry shelf and Nina goes down after it, kneeling in sugar and glass, apologizing to the floor. It isn't about the jar. She looks up at you with something whole and terrible loading behind her eyes — and then you watch her put it away, piece by piece, stand, and ask whether you'd mind collecting the dry cleaning. It costs her everything to say.

choices.text: Gently invite her to talk
choices.consequence: You say her name once, the way you'd say it to someone on a ledge. She almost answers. Then the front door goes, and she is smiling before the sound finishes.

choices.text: Bring her tea and listen
choices.consequence: You make tea nobody drinks and sit through a long silence on the pantry floor beside her. She never says a word. Standing up, she squeezes your wrist — once, hard.

nodes.text: A payroll stub is jammed in the runner of the desk drawer, folded twice, dated fourteen months back. Elena Cruz. Nina told you there had never been anyone before you. Six minutes on your phone in the garage: Elena Cruz, twenty-six, reported missing by a cousin in Yonkers, last known employer withheld. The photo is a driver's licence, and she is smiling like someone who just got a good job.

choices.text: Photograph the stub and hide the photo
choices.consequence: You shoot it, mail it to an account you haven't opened since Bedford Hills, and put the paper back exactly as jammed. Evidence you can't be caught holding.

choices.text: Reach out to the missing maid's family
choices.consequence: You message the cousin from a burner app at midnight. She replies in ninety seconds, which tells you she has spent fourteen months waiting for her phone to do that.

nodes.text: There is a room on the second floor neither of them enters. Nina walks the long way round to avoid its door. The lock is a 1970s privacy latch, the kind a butter knife defeats, and the key hangs in the kitchen on the third hook from the left, between the gate remote and a spare for the shed. A key left that visible is either carelessness or bait.

choices.text: Take the key and look inside
choices.consequence: You lift it on a Tuesday while the dryer covers the sound of the stairs. Whatever is in there, you'd rather know than keep sleeping above it.

choices.text: Wait until you understand the house better
choices.consequence: You leave the key on its hook and spend nine more days learning schedules instead. Patience is a skill you acquired somewhere you don't mention in interviews.

nodes.text: She pulls you into the laundry room and starts the machine before she speaks, which tells you she has done this before, and where. 'He's done it before. He did it to me for six years. I need you to help me and I need you not to decide I'm crazy — he is very good at that part.' Her sleeve rides up. Four ovals on the inside of her wrist, spaced like fingers.

choices.text: Trust her and plan together
choices.consequence: You believe her in the first two seconds and spend the next two deciding not to hide that. Two women in a laundry room, and now there is a plan.

choices.text: Trust her and contact a lawyer for her first
choices.consequence: You believe her and immediately do the unromantic thing: find someone with a bar number. Rescue without paperwork is only a head start.

nodes.text: The locked room turns out to be a nursery — cot, mobile, a decade of dust, a story nobody in this house tells. The cellar is the interesting one. Under the stairs, seven banker's boxes, each with a woman's name in the same neat marker. Elena. Dominika. Rosa. Two you can't read. The dates on the lids run from 2014 to last spring, and none of the writing is Nina's.

choices.text: Photograph everything quickly
choices.consequence: Forty-one photos in six minutes, lids replaced, dust undisturbed, upstairs before the kettle finishes. Your hands shake so badly the last eight come out blurred.

choices.text: Take one box upstairs and confront
choices.consequence: You carry Elena's box up into the light because you are done being careful. It weighs almost nothing, which is somehow the worst detail in it.

nodes.text: You drive into town at lunch and tell a sheriff with a good handshake everything you can prove. He listens well. He writes nothing down. Then he says, 'Andy's a good guy — coached my kid since she was six. Let us handle it,' and walks you to the door with a hand on your back. You are already on the road home before you understand what you filed, and where.

choices.text: Skip town with Nina tonight
choices.consequence: You start counting in hours instead of days. Whatever the sheriff says over dinner tonight, you would rather be past the county line when he says it.

choices.text: Find a different jurisdiction
choices.consequence: You open a map and pick a county where nobody coaches anybody's daughter. It costs you four days you may not have.

nodes.text: The camera in Cecelia's room is aimed at her door, not her bed, and the cable runs through the wall into Andrew's office rather than to any app on Nina's phone. He's been watching who goes in. Standing on the chair to check the angle, you notice the mount is a ball joint. It swivels. It could just as easily be watching something else in this house.

choices.text: Turn it on the master bedroom
choices.consequence: Nine degrees of swivel and a strip of black tape over the indicator light. Whatever he does in that room from Thursday on, he does into a lens.

choices.text: Smash it and pretend it broke
choices.consequence: You kill it with the heel of your shoe and blame the cleaner's ladder. Cecelia sleeps unobserved for the first time in a year, and you lose your best evidence for it.

nodes.text: The power goes at 9:40 and the house becomes a different building — no hum, no fridge, only rain and a generator failing to catch. Andrew is on the stairs with the flashlight held low, and his voice has dropped into a register you have heard exactly once before, at Bedford Hills, from a woman who meant it. 'There's nowhere for you to go.' He's wrong. You have about four minutes to prove it.

choices.text: Get Nina and Cecelia to the car
choices.consequence: You take the child first, coat over her head, and let Nina follow with the cash tin. Three doors, gravel, headlights off until the road.

choices.text: Lure Andrew to the attic and lock him in
choices.consequence: You go up the narrow stairs so he'll follow, because he always follows. The stairs are the trap and you are the bait, and you know exactly which step creaks.

nodes.text: Nina's college roommate is a divorce attorney in the city with a reputation people lower their voices around. She meets you both in a hotel lobby at eight in the morning and does not order coffee. 'Six years,' she says. 'I have kept a folder for six years, Nina.' Then she opens a bag and takes out a file with Nina's married name already printed on the tab.

choices.text: Sign the paperwork; start the protective orders
choices.consequence: Nina signs nine pages in a hotel lobby with a borrowed pen, and her hand only stops shaking on the last one.

choices.text: Push for criminal charges immediately
choices.consequence: You push for handcuffs instead of paperwork. The lawyer warns you that charges are slower and louder — and louder is the one thing a man like Andrew cannot survive.

nodes.text: Two in the morning on I-84, three of you and a cash tin. Cecelia asleep across the back seat with her belt over a stuffed rabbit. Nina reading motel names off a paper list because phones can be followed, saying each one twice like a prayer. You drive four over the limit, mirrors every nine seconds, and understand that you have been rehearsing this exact drive since you were nineteen.

choices.text: Drive across state lines tonight
choices.consequence: You cross at 3:12 and something in your chest unlocks at the sign. New jurisdiction, new sheriff, new set of people who don't coach anybody's kid.

choices.text: Stop at a women's shelter you trust
choices.consequence: You take the exit for a building with no sign on it, because you know the intake nurse there by name. Some addresses you never manage to forget.

nodes.text: He is on the wrong side of a door he paid a man four hundred dollars to install. The banging is arrhythmic and getting worse. You stand in the hall with Cecelia's hand in yours, and she isn't crying — she is listening the way a child listens to weather. The bolt he chose is rated for exterior use. He never once considered which side of it he would be on.

choices.text: Call 911 from the bottom of the stairs
choices.consequence: You dial with the banging audible behind you, so the recording exists whatever anyone claims later. The dispatcher asks you to stay on the line. You stay.

choices.text: Walk out the front door with the women
choices.consequence: You leave him up there with a bolt and a phone within reach, and none of you look back at the house. Nina closes the front door gently. Habit.

nodes.text: The prosecutor two counties over is forty, underslept, and has been building a Winchester file out of nothing for three years. She goes through your photographs twice, stops at the cellar, and says one word: 'Seven.' Then she explains what a box with a name on it becomes in a courtroom, and what your testimony becomes, and what your record becomes when the defense gets to read it aloud.

choices.text: Agree to testify fully
choices.consequence: You agree to a cross-examination that will put Bedford Hills on a screen for twelve jurors. Elena Cruz doesn't get to testify. That's the arithmetic.

choices.text: Negotiate witness protection first
choices.consequence: You ask for a new county and a name that isn't yours before handing over a single page. She respects it. It costs eight weeks.

nodes.text: By seven Cecelia has a bed with a cartoon duvet, Nina has a door that locks from her side, and you are at a laminate table with coffee that tastes like the pot. Three other women sit with you. Nobody asks what happened; everyone already knows the shape of it. One of them slides the sugar over without being asked. That is the entire conversation, and it is enough.

choices.text: Help Nina start over
choices.consequence: You spend four months on her paperwork, her bank account, her daughter's school transfer. Someone has to be the steady one, and you have had practice at being nobody's priority.

choices.text: Decide you need to start over too
choices.consequence: On the third morning you realize you have been running someone else's escape to avoid planning your own. That is a hard thing to admit over bad coffee.

nodes.text: It takes fourteen months. Andrew wears a grey suit and looks like a man being wrongly inconvenienced, right up until the cellar photographs go on the screen. Seven boxes, seven names, seven counts. Nina sells the house to a developer who tears out the attic stairs. Cecelia gets a therapist she likes, a woman with a dog in the office. The jury takes a day and a half.

choices.text: Stay close to the family
choices.consequence: You keep answering the phone when Nina calls at odd hours, and you keep showing up to school concerts you have no legal reason to attend.

choices.text: Move on with what you learned
choices.consequence: You take what the trial taught you about how a house like that recruits, and decide the useful thing isn't staying. It's warning.

nodes.text: She is eighteen at a college fair in a hotel ballroom, holding a lanyard and a stack of pamphlets, and she says your name before you place her face. She's okay. Better than okay — she wants to read law. Out of her bag comes a small framed photograph: three of you at a laminate table, sunrise, terrible coffee. She has carried it for nine years so she could hand it over.

choices.text: Take the photo and the goodbye
choices.consequence: You take the frame, say something inadequate, and let her go back to her pamphlets. Some people you love best by needing nothing from them.

choices.text: Take her to dinner and stay in her life
choices.consequence: You buy her bad ballroom pasta and talk for three hours about admissions essays and restraining orders. She asks more of the second kind of question.

nodes.text: You don't become her mother; Nina is right there, and she is good at it now. You become the other thing — the aunt with no blood in it, the number saved as EMERGENCY-2, the person who drove. Nina remarries a mild man who fixes bicycles. Cecelia grows up loud. The attic door is two thousand miles away in a house that has no attic anymore, and you sleep with both ears, finally.

You start something small out of a rented room: a phone line, four volunteers, a laminated card in three languages that fits in an apron pocket. Rule one on the card — no job requires a door that locks from the outside. In the sixth year a woman calls from a driveway in Connecticut before she has even unpacked, and somebody answers on the second ring. The Winchesters seeded a much better thing without meaning to.
